title: Uniformly bounded algebraic coordinates in a countable-dimensional ultrametric space
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime and let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be finite with its extended nonarchimedean norm [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension]. Let $V\ne0$ be an $E$-vector space with a norm satisfying $\|av\|=|a|\|v\|$ and $\|v+w\|\leq\max(\|v\|,\|w\|)$, with $\|v\|=0$ precisely for $v=0$. Suppose $V$ is spanned algebraically by a finite or countable sequence; no completeness of $V$ is assumed. For any prescribed $v_0\ne0$ there is an algebraic basis $(b_j)_{j\in J}$ (every vector has a unique finite linear expansion) with $0\in J$, $b_0=v_0$, where $J$ is either $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$ for some $d\geq1$ or $\mathbf N$, and constants $0<c\leq C<\infty$ such that for every finitely supported family $(a_j)$ in $E$,
$$c\max_j|a_j|\leq\Big\|\sum_ja_jb_j\Big\|\leq C\max_j|a_j|.$$
The maximum of the empty support is zero. In particular every coordinate projection, every projection onto an arbitrary subset of $J$, and every linear map sending the basis bijectively onto a subset of itself are continuous. The inverse from that coordinate subspace onto $V$ is continuous when the subset is in bijection with $J$. These are algebraic finite-support coordinates, not an assertion about infinite series.

proof.text: Prepend the prescribed vector $v_0\ne0$ to a finite or countable spanning sequence of $V$ and process the resulting sequence in order, starting with $b_0=v_0$; the one-element family $b_0$ satisfies the orthogonality formula $\|a_0b_0\|=|a_0|\|b_0\|$. Inductively, suppose the retained vectors $b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}$ are linearly independent and satisfy $\|\sum_{i<n}a_ib_i\|=\max_{i<n}|a_i|\|b_i\|$, and let $W$ be their span. If the next sequence vector $x$ lies in $W$, discard it. Otherwise [lem-sfb-finite-ultrametric-best-approximation], applied to the finite-dimensional subspace $W$ and $x$, gives $w\in W$ with $\|x-w\|=\inf_{u\in W}\|x-u\|$, and [lem-sfb-ultrametric-orthogonal-extension] shows that $b_n=x-w\ne0$ and that $b_0,\ldots,b_n$ again satisfy the orthogonality formula; retain $b_n$, so that the new span is $W+Ex$. Every finite subfamily of the retained family lies in one stage, so the whole family is linearly independent and satisfies the orthogonality formula on every finite subfamily. Each sequence vector lies in the span of the vectors retained up to its stage, so the retained family spans $V$. It is therefore an algebraic basis; its index set is $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$ with $d\geq1$ when finitely many vectors are retained and $\mathbf N$ otherwise.

proof.text:
For any finitely supported coefficients, the orthogonality formula gives exactly
$$\left\|\sum_j a_jb_j\right\|=\max_j |a_j|\,\|b_j\|.$$ 
This remains valid for the countable case because the support is finite and hence appears at one finite stage of the construction. The empty support gives the zero vector and maximum $0$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), geometric norm-coefficient projection: orthogonal finite-support norm formula.

proof.text:
Put $q=|\ell|_E^{-1}>1$. For every basis vector $b_j$ with $j\ne0$, choose an integer $m_j$ with $q^{m_j}\le\|b_j\|<q^{m_j+1}$ and replace $b_j$ by $\ell^{m_j}b_j$. The replacement preserves the basis and orthogonality, while its norm lies in $[1,q)$. The vector $b_0=v_0$ is left fixed. With $c=\min(\|b_0\|,1)$ and $C=\max(\|b_0\|,q)$, both finite and with $c>0$, the exact formula in the preceding step yields
$$c\max_j|a_j|\le\left\|\sum_j a_jb_j\right\|\le C\max_j|a_j|.$$

source.place: Paragraph (3), geometric norm-coefficient projection: normalization by powers of the uniformizer and uniform constants.

proof.text: The basis expansion is unique by linear independence. The exact norm formula implies each coefficient satisfies $|a_j|\le c^{-1}\|v\|$. Therefore projection onto any subset of coordinates has norm at most $C/c$, and a map that sends each basis vector bijectively onto a subset of the basis has the same bound. If the subset is in bijection with the whole index set, the inverse has the analogous bound, so it is continuous as well. These estimates concern finite algebraic expansions only; no infinite series or completeness assertion is used.
